comments.content: Traversal is asymmetric with `trackEnvVarMappings`, which does recurse into arrays (arrays satisfy `typeof value === 'object'`) and records index-based paths such as `['mcpServers','srv','args','0']`. `restoreEnvVarsRecursive` explicitly skips arrays, so those mappings are never applied and the resolved literal is persisted to disk — exactly the leakage this file exists to prevent for settings with array values (`args`, `includeDirectories`, `excludedProjectEnvVars`, etc.). Add array handling here, e.g. iterate elements and recurse with the index appended to `fullPath`.

Flattening the path with `join('.')` makes the lookup key ambiguous: a settings key that itself contains a dot (`{"a.b": "$X"}`) produces the same key as a nested path (`{"a": {"b": "$X"}}`). MCP server names (used as object keys under `mcpServers`) and keys in `env` blocks are user-supplied strings, so collisions are possible and can cause a `$VAR` reference to be restored at the wrong location, overwriting an unrelated value. Use a structured key (e.g. `JSON.stringify(mapping.path)`) instead of a joined string.

On a parse failure the function logs and returns `void`, indistinguishable from success. `saveSettings` has already mutated the in-memory settings and only wraps the call in a `try/catch` that logs, so the user's change is silently discarded and never persisted, with no way for the caller to react (retry, warn, or fall back). The error contract is also inconsistent: parse errors are swallowed while `readFileSync`/`writeFileSync` failures propagate. Consider returning a boolean/result (or rethrowing a typed error) so callers can report the failure, and document the contract in the JSDoc.

The anchors mean only values that are exactly one reference (`"$TOKEN"`) are preserved. Embedded references such as `"https://$HOST:8080"` or `"${A}-${B}"` (which `resolveEnvVarsInString` does resolve, using a non-anchored global regex) are treated as literals, so their resolved text — potentially a secret — is written back to the settings file on save. This also does not handle `${VAR:-default}` forms. Align the pattern with the resolver (non-anchored, global) and reconstruct the original string by tracking which substrings were substituted.

Both the create branch and the final `fs.writeFileSync` write directly to the target file, so an interrupted process leaves a truncated settings file (no temp-file + `renameSync`, no backup). The `existsSync` + `readFileSync` sequence also leaves a TOCTOU window, and this branch omits the trailing newline that the rest of the file-writing paths produce. Please reuse (or add) an atomic-write helper and append a trailing `\n` for consistency.

The cast asserts the root shape without verification. If the file parses to a top-level array or primitive, `applyUpdates` assigns named properties onto it: on an array those properties are dropped by `JSON.stringify` (producing `[]`, i.e. data loss), and on a primitive in an ESM/strict-mode module the assignment throws. Add a root-shape guard (plain object) and bail out (or treat the file as empty) before merging.

The env-var mappings are recorded against the in-memory (V2) settings shape, but `settingsToSave` is converted to V1 by `migrateSettingsToV1` (because `MIGRATE_V2_OVERWRITE` is `false`) before being handed to the writer. The writer matches mappings by dot path, so every key whose path is renamed by the migration (e.g. `ui.theme` -> `theme`, `security.auth.selectedType` -> `selectedAuthType`, `mcp.serverCommand` -> `mcpServerCommand`) will not match any mapping, and its resolved value - potentially a token embedded in a command - is written literally to disk. Translate the mapping paths to the V1 shape (or restore placeholders before the V1 migration) so the lookup paths line up with the object actually written.

comments.content: `envVarMappings` is captured once at load time and passed unchanged on every subsequent save. The writer replaces *any* string found at a mapped path with the original `${VAR}` placeholder (it ignores the recorded `resolvedValue`), so if the user changes an env-derived setting through `setValue` (e.g. edits `model.name`, an MCP server `env` value, or `preferredEditor`), the new value is merged into the file and then immediately overwritten with the stale placeholder. The user's change silently never persists, and memory/disk diverge. Invalidate the mapping for the key being written, and/or make the writer only restore a placeholder when the current value still equals the recorded resolved value. For whole-object updates such as `mcpServers`, also account for nested mapped keys.
